title: Day 5 — Household Operations, Vendors & Risk Management

frames.title: Day 5 Agenda
frames.text:
Welcome to Day 5: Household Operations, Vendors and Risk Management.

We'll start with running the household, build a Home Binder, then move on to vendors and procurement. The biggest block today is risk management, followed by travel risk, and we'll close with a mid-point review of how the course is going for you.

By the end of today, you'll be able to run household operations like a small business, keep a Home Binder the family can rely on, manage vendors and contracts, and apply a real risk-management framework.

frames.title: Running the Household
frames.text: Section 1 of 6: Running the Household. We'll treat the household like a small business, then look at household staff, home maintenance and personal support.

frames.title: Running a Household Like a Business
frames.text:
A busy household runs smoothly when you treat it like a small business.

Think about how many people touch a busy family's life: a nanny, a housekeeper, contractors, school, doctors. If nobody's coordinating, everyone calls Sarah or Elias.

First, make yourself the main contact for family, staff and contractors. Then, set up simple routines for things that repeat, like bills, staff schedules and maintenance.

frames.title: Running a Household Like a Business
frames.text:
After that, review every so often what's working and what keeps slipping. Finally, write down the household's standing decisions, so things run the same way when you're not there.

Here's a situation to work through. You've just taken over the Thornes' household. There's no shared calendar, the budget is 'in Sarah's head' and vendor numbers are scattered across three phones. What do you build in your first week, and in what order?

frames.title: Recurring Household Admin: Utilities, Purchasing & Subscriptions
frames.text:
If you don't decide before a subscription renews, auto-renew decides for you.

Recurring admin comes in three flavors. Utilities, like power and water, which can never lapse. Purchasing, for work and for home, where it's easy to buy something twice or forget it. And subscriptions, which most people sign up for once and never think about again, until the charge shows up on the statement.

frames.title: Recurring Household Admin: Utilities, Purchasing & Subscriptions
frames.text: First, put every utility payment on a calendar with its real due date. Next, keep a simple record of what's been bought and when. Then, note every subscription's renewal date the day you sign up.

frames.title: Recurring Household Admin: Utilities, Purchasing & Subscriptions
frames.text:
After that, before each renewal, actively decide: keep it or cancel it. Finally, give all three the same attention, even though none feels urgent on any given day.

Think about this. You discover the Thornes pay for three streaming services, two meal-kit subscriptions and a gym nobody uses. How would you review them, and what would you bring to Sarah?

frames.title: Household Staff Management
frames.text:
Write down what's expected of household staff from day one, because verbal agreements drift. By the time there's a disagreement, nobody remembers the original deal the same way.

Managing household staff is mostly coordination, not bossing people around. And a schedule that only works if someone stays late every week isn't sustainable.

frames.title: Household Staff Management
frames.text:
First, keep a short written description of each role: hours, main duties and who they report to. Next, keep a shared calendar of everyone's schedule. Then, have a short, regular check-in, even monthly, to catch small problems early. Finally, keep emergency contacts and basic medical information on file for each staff member.

Think about this. The nanny tells you, only when you ask, that she's been working an extra hour every evening for three weeks because the Thornes come home late. She never mentioned it. What do you do?

frames.title: Home Maintenance & Repair Coordination
frames.text:
Most big, expensive repairs started as a small one that nobody scheduled.

Home maintenance comes in two kinds: routine jobs you can plan, like servicing the heating or clearing gutters, and surprises, like a burst pipe. If you treat them the same way, the routine ones get forgotten and the surprises become panics.

frames.title: Home Maintenance & Repair Coordination
frames.text:
First, build a maintenance calendar for every system with a recommended service schedule. Next, keep a list of trusted tradespeople for each specialty. Then, for any repair, get the scope and cost in writing before work starts, even with someone you trust. Finally, keep warranties and manuals in the Home Binder, so 'is this still covered?' takes seconds.

Here's a situation to work through. At 9 p.m., the housekeeper texts that there's water coming through the kitchen ceiling. Your approval limit for repairs is $1,000, and the emergency plumber quotes $1,800. What do you do tonight?

frames.title: Lifestyle & Personal Support
frames.text:
Your memory can't hold every gift, errand and event. A shared tracker can, with a deadline and an owner for each one. Handling them on the fly works for a week, and then something important slips.

First, log a request the moment it comes in. Then, give each item a clear owner, even if that's you.

frames.title: Lifestyle & Personal Support
frames.text:
After that, check the tracker regularly, so nothing arrives as a last-minute panic. Finally, treat it like any other household system: it only works if you actually use it.

Think about this. You're choosing this year's holiday gift for Elias's biggest client. Last year's gift was a bottle of wine. The client has since stopped drinking. What does your tracker need to show?

frames.title: The Home Binder
frames.text: Section 2 of 6: The Home Binder. What goes in it, how to keep it secure and current, and the digital tools that can hold it.

frames.title: Creating a Home Binder for a Busy Executive
frames.text:
The home binder exists for one moment: when someone else needs critical information and you're not there to tell them. Picture the alarm going off while the nanny is home with the children, and you're unreachable.

A good binder has four parts. How the house runs, with codes, manuals and utility accounts. Family and medical details, like doctors and allergies. Pointers to financial and legal documents. And emergency contacts.

frames.title: Creating a Home Binder for a Busy Executive
frames.text:
First, build the household section. Next, add family and medical. Then, add financial and legal information as pointers only: where to find the policy, not the policy number itself. After that, organize the emergency contacts. Finally, test it: could a substitute or a paramedic use it without calling you?

Here's a way to test yours. The nanny has to find the pediatrician's number, the alarm company and the location of the water shut-off valve in under two minutes, without calling you. What would make that possible, and what usually makes it fail?

frames.title: Home Binder: Format, Security & Maintenance
frames.text:
Should the binder be paper or digital? Paper works when the power or internet is down. Digital is easy to update and reach from anywhere. Most households need both: a digital master, with a printed copy for real emergencies.

First, choose the format based on how it will actually be used. Then, never write sensitive numbers, like account numbers, passwords or ID numbers, in the binder. Write down where to find them instead.

frames.title: Home Binder: Format, Security & Maintenance
frames.text:
After that, update it the moment something changes. Finally, check now and then that nobody has written a sensitive number in by mistake.

Think about this. You're reviewing the Thornes' binder and find the safe combination and a bank account number written on the finance page. What do you change, and where does that information go instead?

frames.title: Digital Home Binder Tools & Platforms
frames.text:
A simple, well-organized tool beats a clever one nobody else can use.

First, if the household already uses a shared workspace, build the binder there. Next, use the same four section headings as a paper binder. Then, set permissions per section. A driver needs the household section, not the family's medical details. Finally, print or export a backup regularly, in case the tool is down.

Here's a situation to work through. The Thornes' previous housekeeper left three months ago, and you discover she can still log into the digital binder, which includes the alarm codes. What do you do today, and what process stops it happening again?

frames.title: Vendors & Procurement
frames.text: Section 3 of 6: Vendors and Procurement. Choosing and managing vendors, negotiating and reading contracts, and what to do when a vendor falls through.

frames.title: Procurement and Vendor/Supplier Management
frames.text:
Choosing a vendor well is what stops vendors from failing you later. It's a sequence, and each step protects the next.

First, look at more than one option. Next, compare more than price: reliability, response time and contract terms. Then, put it in writing: a real contract or statement of work, not a handshake. Finally, keep managing it: track performance and renewal dates, and have a backup ready.

Try this one. A tree-removal company offers to do urgent work tomorrow for cash, with no written quote. They seem friendly and experienced. What do you check before they step onto the property?

frames.title: Vendor Relationships Beyond the Signature
frames.text: Paying a vendor's invoices on time doesn't mean the vendor is doing a good job. The work doesn't stop at signing. You keep watching whether they deliver.

frames.title: Vendor Relationships Beyond the Signature
frames.text: First, compare real options before committing. Next, read the actual terms, not just the price. Then, after signing, check that they're performing.

frames.title: Vendor Relationships Beyond the Signature
frames.text:
After that, track renewal dates like any other recurring admin. Finally, have a backup ready before you need one.

Think about this. The Thornes' pool service has been paid on time every month, but the pool has turned green twice this summer. What should ongoing vendor management have caught, and what do you do now?

frames.title: Negotiating Vendor Contracts & Terms
frames.text:
Your best negotiating tool is a real alternative lined up before you start. A vendor who knows you have no other option has no reason to budge. And most vendors' standard contracts are more flexible than people think, especially on payment, cancellation and service guarantees.

First, know what matters most to you, in order: price, timing, flexibility or guarantees. Next, ask for better terms on at least one thing besides price, like a shorter cancellation notice. Then, get everything you agree into the written contract. Finally, renegotiate at renewal instead of letting it roll over automatically.

Think about this. A vendor the family has used happily for two years sends a renewal with a 15 percent increase and no explanation. You have one untested alternative. How do you approach the conversation?

frames.title: Reading a Contract: The Clauses to Recognize
frames.text:
You'll handle contracts every week, and the costly mistakes hide in a few clauses with dates in them.

We don't decide what a contract should say. That's the attorney's job. But we do need to recognize the parts. Most contracts have the same building blocks: who the parties are, what's being provided, payment, how long it lasts and whether it renews, how it can be ended, confidentiality, indemnification, which is who covers whose losses, limits on liability, insurance, which state's law applies, and the signatures.

frames.title: Reading a Contract: The Clauses to Recognize
frames.text: First, we read the first page for the parties and date, then find the term: start, end and automatic renewal. Next, we find every notice period and put a reminder in the calendar before each one. Then we note payment terms and scope, so invoices can be checked.

frames.title: Reading a Contract: The Clauses to Recognize
frames.text:
After that, we write a one-page summary for the file. Finally, the contract goes to the attorney before signing, with anything unusual flagged.

Pause the video and work this one out. A three-year catering contract says it 'renews automatically for successive one-year terms unless either party gives 90 days' written notice.' It started March 1, 2024. When is the last day to give notice, and what goes in the calendar?

frames.title: When a Vendor Falls Through
frames.text:
When a vendor lets you down, the worst thing you can do is try to fix it quietly while the clock runs down. The best thing is to be the first to say what's happened and what you propose to do about it.

First, tell the household right away. Next, offer specific alternatives in the same message. Then, go to your pre-checked backup vendor, not a cold search.

frames.title: When a Vendor Falls Through
frames.text:
After that, confirm the backup can actually deliver in time, so one failure doesn't become two. Finally, once it's resolved, update the vendor records.

Take a second with this one. The caterer for Sarah Thorne's dinner party for 20 cancels at 2 p.m. on the day. What do you do in the first five minutes, and what does your message to Sarah say?

frames.title: Vendor NDA Management
frames.text:
Some vendors see private household or business information. For them, the NDA gets signed first, and access comes second. But it doesn't end at signing.

First, decide which vendors really need an NDA, based on what they'll see. Next, keep a simple record of who has signed, when and what it covers. Finally, check it again whenever the vendor's work expands.

Think about this. The home IT technician's work grows from setting up Wi-Fi to reorganizing the family's personal files. The original NDA only covered network setup. What do you do?

frames.title: Risk Management
frames.text: Section 4 of 6: Risk Management. We'll start with the framework and the four core risk strategies, then work through the specific risks an EA or PA manages, like information security.

frames.title: The PA Risk Management Framework
frames.text:
Risk in a household falls into four groups. Money risk, like a missed insurance premium or fraud. Legal risk, like someone getting hurt on the property. Operational risk, like a vendor who doesn't show up. And reputation risk, like a family matter ending up on social media.

The trick is that real incidents rarely stay in just one group, so look at all of them.

frames.title: The PA Risk Management Framework
frames.text: First, for financial risk, keep an eye on renewals and confirm payments went through. Next, for legal risk, notice injury, contract or staff issues as they come up. Then, for operational risk, have backup plans ready before something goes wrong.

frames.title: The PA Risk Management Framework
frames.text:
After that, for reputational risk, make discretion a daily habit. Finally, when something happens, check it against all four, not just the obvious one.

Here's a situation to work through. A delivery driver slips on the Thornes' icy driveway and posts about it on social media. Map it to every risk category it touches, and say what you'd do first.

frames.title: The Four Core Risk Strategies
frames.text:
There are only four ways to handle a risk: avoid it, reduce it, insure it or accept it.

First, avoid: if a risk can reasonably be skipped, skip it. Next, reduce: if you can't avoid it, lower it, with alarms, training or safer driving. Then, transfer: if the money at stake is big, move it to an insurer.

frames.title: The Four Core Risk Strategies
frames.text:
After that, retain: if insuring costs more than the risk itself, accept it on purpose. Finally, choose the approach for each specific risk, rather than using the same one for everything.

Pause the video and try this. Match a strategy to each risk: a leaky pool fence with young children in the house, a $3,000 painting, the family's annual trip to Europe and a scratch-prone rental car.

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. A family purchases homeowners insurance to cover potential losses from fire or theft. Which risk strategy is this? Is it A, transfer, B, retention, C, reduction, or D, avoidance?

Take a second.

The answer is A, transfer. Buying insurance shifts the financial risk onto the insurer.

frames.title: Insurance & Risk at a Glance
frames.text:
Insurance written years ago may not fit the family's life today.

Families change: they buy property, have children, hire staff and travel more. Your job is to track every policy and check twice a year whether the coverage still matches their life.

frames.title: Insurance & Risk at a Glance
frames.text: First, keep a secure policy tracker: type, insurer, policy number, who's covered, deductible, premium and renewal date. Next, watch every renewal date, so nothing lapses. Then, compare what they have with what they now need.

frames.title: Insurance & Risk at a Glance
frames.text:
After that, at each review, ask: new property or car? Marriage or divorce? New dependents? Business changes? More wealth? Tell the broker about every yes. Finally, treat each yes as a gap to close, not a note for later.

Try it on the Thornes. In the last six months they bought a lake house, hired a full-time nanny and started traveling abroad every quarter. Which gaps do you flag?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. During the semi-annual risk review, which of these is a genuine trigger to revisit coverage? Is it A, a vendor changed their logo, B, the assistant took a vacation, C, net worth increased significantly since the last review, or D, the weather changed?

Take a second.

It's C. A meaningful change in net worth, property, vehicles or household staff should always prompt a coverage check.

frames.title: EA/PA Risk Framework: Information Security
frames.text:
A confident-sounding request is not the same as a verified one.

You see more private information than almost anyone around the executive, so information security is your job, not just IT's.

First, only access and keep the sensitive information you actually need. Next, confirm who you're talking to before sharing anything sensitive by phone or email. Then, use secure channels, never casual texts. Finally, know what to do if something leaks: stop it spreading, work out how much got out and escalate. Blame can wait.

Think about this. An email that looks like it's from Elias's bank asks you to confirm his account details to clear a 'security flag.' It arrived at an odd time. What do you do before replying?

frames.title: EA/PA Risk Framework: Operational Continuity
frames.text:
Being the only person who knows how to do something isn't job security. It's a risk.

Operational continuity means essential things keep happening even when you're sick, a system goes down or a key vendor fails. The SOPs, the binder and the contact list you've been building are all continuity tools.

First, list the tasks that would actually break if you were unreachable for 48 hours. Next, write those processes down briefly, so someone else could do them. Then, have a backup contact for every critical vendor and system. Finally, create a simple 'if I'm unreachable' plan, and make sure someone knows it exists.

Think about this. A temp tries to follow the continuity plan you wrote six months ago. The alarm company number is wrong and two vendors have changed. What do you change about how you keep the plan current?

frames.title: EA/PA Risk Framework: Reputational Risks
frames.text:
Assume anything you write could one day be seen by people it wasn't meant for. Reputational damage spreads faster and lasts longer than most other problems, so your role is mostly preventive.

First, make discretion your default for anything that could go public. Next, look at guest lists, appearances and social posts with reputation in mind, not just logistics. Then, know who needs to hear first if something goes wrong, and who is allowed to speak publicly. Finally, control what gets shared, with whom and when.

Think about this. A journalist contacts you directly, outside the firm's usual channels, asking for comment on a sensitive matter involving Elias. What do you do, and what do you deliberately avoid?

frames.title: EA/PA Risk Framework: Physical & Travel Safety
frames.text:
Physical safety is the one risk where a gap can't be undone.

This is about real, physical danger to the executive or family, whether traveling, at events or in daily life. Duty of care means knowing where someone is and being able to reach or help them.

frames.title: EA/PA Risk Framework: Physical & Travel Safety
frames.text:
First, always know where the executive is during travel or high-profile events, without being intrusive. Next, before an unfamiliar or riskier trip, learn the local emergency numbers, the nearest hospital and any advisories. Then, work with security staff, not around them. Finally, keep emergency and basic medical information where you can find it in seconds.

Try this one. Elias's daughter is traveling alone to a summer program abroad, and she's agreed to check in by text every evening. On day three, there's no message by midnight. What was agreed in advance, and what do you do now?

frames.title: EA/PA Risk Framework: Financial Controls
frames.text:
You probably approve invoices, manage accounts or handle reimbursements, so financial controls are part of your job. And they protect you too: clear limits and records mean it's never your word against someone else's.

First, know your approval limit in actual dollars before you need it. Next, require paperwork for every transaction, even the small ones. Then, reconcile recurring spending at least monthly. Finally, flag anything unusual straight away, even if you're not sure it's wrong.

Try this one. A text from an unknown number says: 'It's Sarah, new phone. Please send $4,000 to this account for the kitchen contractor, I'm in a meeting.' What do you do in the next ten minutes?

frames.title: Private Expense Audit
frames.text:
Processing each charge as it comes in isn't the same as reviewing them. Odd charges are much easier to spot when you look at a month together. It's the same reconciliation habit from financial controls, applied to the family's personal spending.

First, set a regular review, usually monthly. Next, compare what was charged with what you expected: subscriptions, contracts and staff pay. Finally, flag anything unclear rather than assuming it's fine.

Think about this. The monthly review shows a $450 charge at a jewelry store that nobody has mentioned. How do you raise it without implying anyone did something wrong?

frames.title: Travel Risk
frames.text: Section 5 of 6: Travel Risk. Managing risk before, during and after a trip, handling a travel claim, and duty of care abroad.

frames.title: Travel Risk Management
frames.text:
Travel safety has three phases, before, during and after, and each has its own job.

Before the trip, we confirm travel insurance and medical cover abroad, and for high-profile trips we register with the embassy. During it, the traveler has an emergency contact sheet, copies of key documents and safe Wi-Fi habits. And after it, we reconcile expenses and file any claims while the details are still fresh.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias is in Mexico City and his phone has been stolen. What should already be on his printed emergency sheet, and who does he call first?

frames.title: Handling a Travel Claim
frames.text:
When something goes wrong on a trip, the order is safety, evidence and never admitting fault. A travel claim isn't just paperwork; it's a risk event. You're the coordinator, the keeper of the documents and the link to the executive.

First, make sure everyone is safe, and call emergency services if needed. Then, preserve evidence immediately: photos, damaged items, report numbers and witness details.

frames.title: Handling a Travel Claim
frames.text:
After that, never admit fault on the executive's behalf, however it looks in the moment. Finally, only once things are safe, move on to the forms and the claim.

Think about this. Elias's rental car is rear-ended in Lisbon, and the other driver insists it was his fault. He calls you from the roadside. What do you tell him to do, and in what order?

frames.title: International Travel Risk & Duty of Care
frames.text:
Duty of care means knowing where a traveler is and being able to reach them if something goes wrong. International travel brings risks home travel doesn't: political unrest, weaker health systems, unfamiliar laws and language barriers. The riskier the place, the more planning has to happen before departure.

First, check official travel advisories before booking, not just before leaving. Next, register the trip with the government's travel program where one exists. Then, confirm international health cover, and for riskier places, medical evacuation insurance. Finally, make a destination emergency card: embassy, hospital, local emergency numbers and a check-in schedule.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias's daily check-in on an international trip is set for 8 p.m. local time. It's now 10 p.m. with no word, and his phone goes to voicemail. What was your agreed plan, and what do you do next?

frames.title: Mid-Point Review
frames.text: Section 6 of 6: Mid-Point Review. A one-on-one look at how the first half of the course has gone for you.

frames.title: Mid-Point 1-on-1 Performance Review
frames.text:
We're halfway through, and this is the best moment to fix anything that still feels shaky. This review is a two-way conversation, not a verdict.

First, come in with an honest view of which days and tools feel solid and which still feel shaky. Next, use the real data: Knowledge Check scores, Practice Lab history and roleplay results. Finally, leave with one specific focus for the second half, not a vague 'try harder.'

Take a moment with this. Look honestly at Days 1 to 5. Which day or Practice Lab tool would you most like to revisit, and what exactly still feels unclear?

frames.title: Practice Lab
frames.text: Now it's your turn. In today's Practice Lab, the Household Risk Assessment, you'll classify the risks facing the Thorne family, match each one to the right risk-management strategy, build a real Home Binder section, and then handle a live crisis roleplay drawn from real household scenarios.
